title: Topology versus geometry
confusion: A reader can think the course is choosing topology and rejecting geometry. That misses the working pattern: geometry often supplies the small local fact, while topology says which completed accounts are possible after the object is allowed to move.
left_job: Topology asks what survives when exact measurement is allowed to change: routes, holes, boundaries, side behavior, fixed points, and total constraints. Its job is to protect the part of the situation that still answers the question after stretching, redrawing, or changing coordinates.
right_job: Geometry keeps measured local information in view: length, angle, direction, curvature, and local bending. Those facts often become the pieces that a topological account adds up, compares, or forces to appear somewhere on the whole object.
bridge: The course often starts geometrically and ends topologically. A local arrow turns, a curve meets another curve, or a surface bends; then the whole shape restricts the total account. The two sides cooperate when the page says which local measurement is being kept and which global rule makes that local evidence matter.
failure_test: If the explanation says measurement never matters, it has lost geometry. If it says only measurement matters, it has lost the reason whole-shape constraints can force an answer. A good repair names both levels: the local measured fact and the whole object that controls its total behavior.
reader_question: Which local measured fact is present, which whole-shape fact controls what that local evidence can do, and what would change if the exact measurement were allowed to vary?

title: Invariant versus raw count
confusion: A visible number can look like evidence just because it is easy to count. The course repeatedly shows that easy counts may change under harmless redrawings, so the number by itself is not yet a reason.
left_job: An invariant is chosen because it survives the allowed moves. It carries the answer from one version of the picture to another. Its value comes from the survival proof, not from the fact that it is numerical.
right_job: A raw count is what the eye sees in one drawing: crossings, cells, regions, or defects before the legal changes have been tested. It may be a useful starting material, but it has not yet earned the right to speak for every legal version of the situation.
bridge: The raw count becomes evidence only after it is repaired. Alternating signs, parity, or plus-minus cancellation can turn an unstable count into protected evidence. The bridge is the local audit: show what happens when a harmless change creates, removes, or rearranges visible events.
failure_test: If the count changes during a legal move and the explanation has no cancellation rule, the count is not yet an invariant. A repaired explanation says exactly which local changes threaten the number and why the chosen account ignores or cancels those threats.
reader_question: What local change threatens the count, what part of the count survives that change, and why is that surviving part enough to force the conclusion?

title: Deformation versus illegal shortcut
confusion: A cleaner drawing can feel like progress even when the cleanup changed the problem. This is the main danger in visual topology: the final picture may be easier to inspect but no longer answer the starting question.
left_job: A deformation is a continuous legal change that preserves the question being asked. It lets an easier picture speak for the harder one because every step carried the protected feature along with it.
right_job: An illegal shortcut cuts, crosses, jumps, moves fixed data, drops a boundary, or changes the state space while pretending the answer is still about the original problem. It can produce a beautiful final drawing and still be mathematically irrelevant.
bridge: The difference is the rulebook. The same visible motion may be legal in one problem and forbidden in another, so the allowed move has to be named before the simplification is trusted. The proof is the route, not only the before-and-after pair.
failure_test: If a curve passes through a forbidden obstacle or an endpoint quietly changes order, the proof has solved a different problem. A repair must identify the illegal moment and either forbid it or change the claim to match the new rulebook.
reader_question: What changed during the motion, what exact feature was protected at every step, and which tempting simplification would break that protection?

title: Quotient space versus drawing
confusion: A square with arrows can be mistaken for a square. In the course, the arrows are instructions for what the finished space actually is, so the flat drawing is a code rather than the final object.
left_job: A quotient space declares certain points to be the same point. That declaration creates the routes, neighborhoods, and side behavior of the finished object. The mathematical object is born when the identification rule is applied.
right_job: A drawing is only a readable code for the rule. Its visible boundary or flat outline may not be a true boundary or shape in the completed space. The ink helps the reader remember the instructions, but it does not overrule them.
bridge: Read the rule before reading the picture. Once the identifications are applied, travel, orientation, and boundary behavior may change. The bridge is a translation step: ask what happens to a small traveler after the marked edges are glued.
failure_test: If the explanation reasons on the unglued drawing after the identification rule has been stated, it is using the wrong object. A repair says which edge, point, or neighborhood was identified before drawing conclusions about paths or sides.
reader_question: Which points have been identified, what path or boundary behavior changes after that identification, and which feature of the flat drawing is no longer literal?

title: Product space versus configuration space
confusion: Both can sound like spaces of choices. Product space records independent choices before later restrictions are imposed; configuration space must represent the actual allowed states of a system after its real restrictions are included.
left_job: A product space keeps separate choices together. One point records a tuple of choices before any later constraints are imposed. It is the first model to try when several freedoms are being chosen at once.
right_job: A configuration space records complete allowed states of a system. It may start from product choices, but then forbidden states, walls, or equations must be removed or imposed. It is the model that the theorem actually sees.
bridge: Many models start with a product and become a configuration space only after the real restrictions are added. The topology speaks about the restricted state space, not the larger wishful one. Collisions, locked positions, and missing rotations cannot be treated as afterthoughts because they change the space the theorem sees.
failure_test: If the model includes collisions or impossible positions because it stopped at the product, it may erase the obstruction the application depends on. If it removes a real freedom, it may invent an obstruction that the physical system does not have.
reader_question: Which choices vary independently, which states must be removed before the model represents the real system, and which theorem claim depends on the restricted space rather than the product draft?

title: Generic position versus special accident
confusion: A special drawing can look more informative because it has tangencies, perfect alignments, or multiple events at once. The course often moves away from that drawing because the exact coincidence can hide the stable behavior on either side.
left_job: Generic position gives a clean ordinary case where meetings are separated, defects are isolated, and signs or counts can be assigned. It is not a refusal to study exceptions; it is a way to make the ordinary mechanism visible before returning to the exception.
right_job: A special accident is a fragile coincidence. It may mark a transition, but it can hide the ordinary events on either side. A tangency, double event, or non-isolated defect needs interpretation through nearby stable pictures.
bridge: Study the ordinary case first, then use the special accident as the moment where ordinary events are born, die, or change in controlled pairs. The bridge is the tiny legal nudge: it reveals what count or sign rule the exact accident was concealing.
failure_test: If the small nudge changes the protected fact, generic position has been misused. If no nudge is made, the count may not be defined. A repair must say both why the nudge is legal and what evidence becomes readable after the nudge.
reader_question: What accident was removed, what ordinary count or sign rule became available afterward, and why did the small move preserve the question?

title: Fixed point versus equilibrium
confusion: Both sound like something staying put. The course uses them differently: one belongs to a rule sending points to points, the other belongs to an arrow field or motion law. The shared feeling of stillness is not enough to identify the object.
left_job: A fixed point is an input that a rule sends back to itself. The graph-and-diagonal picture turns self-agreement into an intersection: the rule's output meets the original point. The theorem may prove that such a point exists without finding it.
right_job: An equilibrium is a place where an arrow field vanishes. Nearby arrows show how motion fails around that place. The surrounding arrow pattern, not only the dot, gives the local index evidence.
bridge: Both are forced special states, but their evidence differs. Fixed points use self-agreement of a map; equilibria use local arrow behavior and index. The course bridge is that topology can force a special state before direct computation, but the proof must name which kind of state it is forcing.
failure_test: If the explanation uses fixed-point language for a vector-field defect without naming the arrow field, or uses equilibrium language for a map without a motion law, the object has been blurred. A repair starts by naming either the self-map or the vector field.
reader_question: Is the course studying a rule that returns points, or an arrow field whose arrows vanish, and what evidence forces the special state in that setting?

title: Vector-field index versus Euler characteristic
confusion: Both are numbers in Poincare-Hopf, but they live on different sides of the account. One is read from the arrow field near defects; the other is read from the surface as a completed carrier.
left_job: Vector-field index is local evidence. It counts how arrows turn around one isolated defect. Each defect contributes its own signed local account, and the proof needs the full list before a global sum can be trusted.
right_job: Euler characteristic is whole-surface evidence. It comes from the surface's global bookkeeping, independent of one arrow pattern. It is the number the surface brings to the theorem before any particular defect is inspected.
bridge: Poincare-Hopf connects them by adding every local index and comparing the total to the Euler characteristic of the same surface. The theorem turns many local arrow failures into one surface-wide accounting rule.
failure_test: If one defect is compared directly to Euler characteristic, or if the surface in the index account is not the surface whose Euler characteristic is used, the theorem has been misread. A repair names all defects, the surface carrying them, and the equality between total index and surface count.
reader_question: Which local indices are being added, which whole surface supplies the Euler characteristic they must match, and what assumption lets those two accounts be compared?

title: Boundary versus hole
confusion: Both can feel like missing space in a drawing, but they affect arguments in different ways. A boundary is part of the object with rules attached; a hole is absent filling that can block a route or deformation.
left_job: A boundary is where the surface stops or where extra edge behavior must be counted. It can add conditions or terms to the argument, and it can decide whether a local direction or cancellation rule is complete.
right_job: A hole is an absent region or blocked filling. It can prevent a loop from shrinking or a path from escaping. The important fact is not empty-looking space, but the route obstruction created by what cannot be crossed or filled.
bridge: Both change what routes and counts are legal. The reader has to ask whether the issue is an edge that contributes data or a missing region that blocks a move. Some examples involve both, so the page must say which job each feature is doing.
failure_test: If an edge is ignored as though the surface had no boundary, or if a hole is treated like a removable drawing feature, the proof can lose the obstruction. A repair says whether the feature contributes a boundary term, blocks a filling, or changes the allowed motion.
reader_question: Is the argument using an edge condition, a missing filling region, or both at the same time, and what legal move would fail if the feature were removed?

title: Source support versus source overclaim
confusion: A reference can support a family of ideas without proving every sentence on a course page. The danger is to treat citation as a blanket permission instead of asking what exact claim the source can carry.
left_job: Source support ties a course move to the course videos, a primary-paper family, or a standard reference for the background mathematics. Its job is limited: identify the course, support a broader theorem family, or clarify formal background after the lecture object is already plain.
right_job: Source overclaim treats a reference as if it directly proves a lecture interpretation, exact wording, or stronger theorem use that the available source evidence does not justify. It hides the difference between caption evidence, visible demonstration, course-arc inference, and background mathematics.
bridge: The companion should move from lecture evidence to source family carefully: course demonstration first, source support second, caveat always visible. A useful source sentence says whether it is supporting provenance, history, formal theorem background, or a course-specific claim.
failure_test: If a sentence would become false or too strong when the auto-caption caveat is remembered, it is probably overclaiming. A repair weakens the claim or adds the missing label: caption support, visible demonstration, course inference, or background-source support.
reader_question: What exact claim does the source support, what stronger claim should remain unsaid, and what evidence type is doing the work?
